title: TMPO promotes cellular dissemination and metastasis in circulating tumor cells
abstract: Metastasis-the process by which cancer cells spread beyond the primary tumor to distant organs-accounts for the vast majority of cancer-related deaths. To elucidate mechanisms underlying dissemination and metastasis in prostate cancer, we have investigated circulating tumor cells (CTCs) obtained from genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs). The phenotypic and molecular properties of the CTCs, and organoids derived from these CTCs, closely model the tumor and metastatic phenotypes of their parental GEMMs. Moreover, organoids derived from individual CTCs exhibit molecular and morphological heterogeneity that is associated with distinct metabolic states as well as differences in human prostate cancer outcome. Using computational systems analyses, we have identified TMPO , encoding the nuclear membrane protein lamina-associated polypeptide 2 (Lap2), as a key driver of this heterogeneity. TMPO activity is upregulated in advanced human prostate tumors, metastases, and CTCs, and is associated with adverse clinical outcome. Our findings indicate that TMPO promotes dissemination and metastasis in vivo by enhancing survival in conditions of metabolic stress, and reveal a novel mechanistic link between CTC heterogeneity, stress adaptation, and metastatic potential.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This 2025 preprint on prostate cancer metastasis already shows early downstream reuse: it is indexed as a biomedical article mention in Europe PMC and has two documented mentions in scite. The record is otherwise still early, with no OpenAlex citations yet and no tracked public discussion, so its influence is best described as emerging rather than established.

Full narrative

TMPO promotes cellular dissemination and metastasis in circulating tumor cells is a bioRxiv preprint from a large, multi-institution team spanning Columbia University, Cornell University, and other research institutions. The study focuses on circulating tumor cells in prostate cancer, using genetically engineered mouse models and CTC-derived organoids to investigate the phenotypic and molecular features associated with dissemination and metastatic behavior. Supported by multiple NIH awards, the work is positioned squarely within current metastasis research and cancer biology.

The strongest impact signals in the record are early but concrete forms of reuse. Europe PMC indexes the work as a biomedical article mention, and scite records two mentions of the preprint. Those signals indicate that the paper is already entering the scholarly conversation, even before citation accumulation has had time to build.

At the same time, the broader attention profile remains sparse. OpenAlex shows no citations yet, Event Data reports no online mentions, and the public-discourse archive is unavailable in this record. That combination suggests the article is still in the first phase of dissemination: visible to specialist indexing services and reuse trackers, but not yet reflected in wider citation or public engagement metrics.

Taken together, the article’s current footprint is best understood as an emerging research contribution with clear relevance to metastatic prostate cancer biology. Its near-term significance lies less in accumulated impact metrics and more in the fact that it has already been reused and surfaced in biomedical indexing, which can be an early indicator of uptake as the work moves from preprint to more mature scholarly circulation.
